INDUSTRY PERSPECTIVE

Autonomy is a workflow question.

Why buyers should ask when people help, what they do, and how often intervention is needed.

H
HUMANOID EditorialResearch, hardware & practical perspectives
EDITORIAL DATE6 Jul 20262 min read

Manufacturer imagery used for editorial illustration. A product image does not imply affiliation or a hands-on review.

IN THIS STORY
01Break the task into stages02Make interventions measurable03Understand the connection requirements04Keep progress claims specific→Your next stepExplore hardware ↗
THE KEY IDEA

Describe human involvement explicitly instead of assigning one autonomy label to an entire robot.

A robot may perform one action independently, ask for help on another, and use remote control during setup. A single word such as autonomous cannot explain that whole operating model. For buyers and developers, the useful question is where people enter the workflow and what their involvement requires.

01

Break the task into stages

Consider setup, perception, task execution, exception handling, and recovery separately. Ask which stages are automatic and which need an operator. A system can be useful with human assistance, provided that assistance is understood and included in the operating plan.

02

Make interventions measurable

Record the number, duration, and cause of interventions during a representative trial. Include help given before a task starts or after a failure, not only direct control during motion. Those records create a clearer basis for estimating staffing and evaluating improvements over time.

03

Understand the connection requirements

Where remote assistance is part of the design, ask how connectivity, permissions, and service availability affect operation. Discuss what the system does when the connection is interrupted. For projects using cameras or microphones, establish the organization’s expectations for access and recording before the trial.

04

Keep progress claims specific

A reduction in help for one object set is valuable, but it should be described with the conditions that produced it. Avoid expanding a narrow result into a claim about every environment. A precise account of the task and intervention pattern is more useful than a broad statement about intelligence.

MAKE IT PRACTICAL

Your next step.

  • Map human involvement by task stage.
  • Count both visible and background interventions.
  • Confirm the operating model when connectivity is unavailable.
